output.headline: UK unveils Be Ready campaign to help households prepare for emergencies
output.bodyHtml:
The government has launched a new Be Ready campaign, urging every person to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food, in guidance designed to help families survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.

The campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.

Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.

Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.

The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.

People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.

“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.

“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.

Related: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn

“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”

Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.

There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.

The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.

Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.

People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.

The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.

Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.

European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.

Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.
output.standfirst: The Cabinet Office's new campaign tells people to stock three days of water, food and essentials each, as ministers address risks from storms, cyber-attacks and hostile states.
output.progress: Dan Jarvis and Wes Streeting say the campaign improves national resilience against storms, cyber-attacks and hostile-state sabotage.

output.headline: Government to weigh 200,000 responses before finalising migration reform
output.bodyHtml:
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising planned changes to migration policy.

Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Andy Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.

“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”

Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

Mahmood is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards. She has previously hinted that the plan could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.

MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.

Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.

“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has clarified that she backs Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.

Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.

She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”

The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 declined to say whether they had asked her to issue a clarification.

Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.

“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”

The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.

However, there were reports on Tuesday that Mahmood was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”

This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”

And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.

Related: Home Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 years
output.standfirst: Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh clarified she backs the policy after joking she could not 'lie' about supporting it, amid a cabinet split over plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years for residency
output.progress: Mahmood is weighing whether to exempt care workers from the new rule after MPs raised concerns about staff shortages.

output.headline: Guardian investigation reveals billionaire Reform donor's Iran-linked business ties
output.bodyHtml:
Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.

Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.

He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.

The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.

Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.

It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.

Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.

The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.

The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.

The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.

AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.

The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.

The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.

Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”

He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.

The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.

Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.

The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.

According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.

In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.

Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.

Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.

Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.

In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.

It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.

In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.

At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.
output.standfirst: Sasan Ghandehari's past business partnership with an Iranian religious foundation under the supreme leader's authority raises questions about his dealings with the hardline republic, which Nigel Farage has strongly criticised.

output.headline: Chancellor to unveil 'breathing space' measures in the budget
output.bodyHtml:
Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also acknowledged that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.

With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

Related: Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urged

The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.

Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.

Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month, while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.

In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.

According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.

The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.

Related: Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeeze

Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.

Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.

Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.

“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”

The Treasury has been approached for comment.
output.standfirst: John Healey has promised ‘breathing space’ measures in next week’s budget, after GfK found UK consumer confidence fell at its fastest rate since the Covid pandemic amid the cost-of-living squeeze.
output.progress: The CBI is urging the chancellor to cut business electricity costs and reform business rates to support investment.

context.text: UK GDP grew 0.1% in August, defying forecasts of a contraction, even as the Middle East war squeezed household spending.

output.headline: Doctors call for climate action and better heat protection across Europe
output.bodyHtml:
Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes.

Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research suggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths.

Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.

The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.

“In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.”

The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found.

People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death.

“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.”

In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks.

The “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further.

“We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.”

The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages.

The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring service announced this month, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record.

Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall.

The study combined established relationships between heat and mortality with temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods.

David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said.

“The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”
output.standfirst: Doctors are urging governments to cut emissions and strengthen heat protections, after new research found heat killed a record 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, with climate breakdown blamed for two in three deaths.
output.progress: Doctors are urging governments to cut emissions, strengthen health systems and roll out cooling measures, and residents to check on vulnerable neighbours.

output.headline: Judge holds Trump to same discovery rules as any other litigant in BBC case
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.

Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.

“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom.

The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.

“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”

The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.

Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”

After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned to the BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition, after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.

While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.

Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.

“The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said.

In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January.

During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president.

Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.”

Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.”

In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.

“I think it is intertwined with his profession and therefore any harm that may be alleged under his professional trade and occupation would be reflected with how he conducts business with Mar-a-Lago, at least for discovery purposes,” she added.
output.standfirst: A Miami judge has ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by 11 December, saying his team could face dismissal of the $10bn BBC lawsuit if they keep stalling discovery.
output.progress: The judge also let the BBC's subpoena to Trump's Mar-a-Lago club go ahead, ruling it relevant to the case.

output.headline: Liechtenstein prince opens door to lifting abortion information ban
output.bodyHtml:
In his statement this week, Alois also said he was open to lifting the nationwide ban on information about abortion, suggesting that women might one day be able to consult their healthcare provider on where to access the procedure abroad and receive support afterwards.

The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein has used his veto for the first time in his reign to quash a bill aimed at bringing abortion laws in line with much of Europe.

The legislation was approved by Liechtenstein’s parliament last month after the presentation of a citizens’ initiative signed by roughly a quarter of the nation’s voters.

The news left campaigners in the principality, home to some of the strictest abortion laws in Europe, reeling. “We’re not really surprised, but still disappointed,” said Tatjana As’Ad, who led the initiative to overhaul the law and who works for the small leftwing party, Free List. “It’s surreal what’s happening right now in 2026 in a state in the middle of Europe.”

The veto would do little to actually prevent abortions from taking place, she said. “Liechtenstein will continue to have a situation where abortions are banned, but we know they’re happening. The veto just means they will continue to take place abroad.”

Related: Poland’s parliament votes to ease abortion ban but faces likely veto from president

Abortions in the principality are allowed only in limited circumstances such as when a woman’s life is at risk or a pregnancy is the result of rape. Since 2015, women have been legally permitted to travel abroad to terminate a pregnancy to skirt around the restrictions.

After campaigners launched the citizen’s initiative in February, more than 4,970 people – far more than the 1,000 signatures needed to send it to parliament – backed the call to decriminalise abortion up to 12 weeks. The initiative also called for the procedure to be covered by health insurance and for a repeal of a nationwide ban on sharing information about abortion access.

The hope was to do away with the many barriers that women face by being forced to travel abroad, often to neighbouring Austria or Switzerland, which include the cost, the need to arrange childcare and the lack of a vehicle.

As the initiative gained steam, Liechtenstein’s hereditary prince, Alois, said he would use his veto to counter any overhaul of the laws. The promise loomed over the initiative, even as parliamentarians voted narrowly to back it and an August poll suggested that 62% of voters were in favour of reforming the law.

This week the royal house confirmed Alois’s decision to “withhold his sanction from the bill” in a statement. It said: “Following careful consideration, he remains convinced that the proposed reform is not compatible with ensuring adequate protection of unborn life as a fundamental legal value.”

The royal house did not respond to a further request for comment from the Guardian.

Campaigners, who said they had met Alois hours before he announced his decision, described it as a blow to Liechtenstein’s identity as a monarchy underpinned by democratic principles.

“A single individual is overriding a decision initiated by almost a quarter of eligible voters and passed by the parliament,” the committee behind the citizens’ initiative said in a statement.

“Hereditary Prince Alois has only threatened to veto legislation twice in his reign, and both times it concerned the legalisation of abortion,” the statement added, referring to a 2011 pronouncement by the regent.

“This is the first time he has actually exercised this veto. The conclusion is clear: when it comes to abortion, there is only one decision-maker.”

It was a nod to the tremendous power the monarchy holds over the Alpine nation, with the ruling prince able to appoint judges and fire the government or individual ministers, said Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel, a journalist and one of the campaigners behind the citizens’ initiative. “He has a veto over everything, really,” she said.

In 2012, voters cast their ballots overwhelmingly to uphold his veto powers, in a referendum that was described at the time as a proxy debate over whether or not Liechtenstein should have a monarchy.

Related: The abortion debate has gone quiet amid US midterms. In Idaho, the stakes remain high

Alvarez-Hummel described this week’s decision as “very troubling”, given that Liechtenstein was the last in Europe to grant women the right to vote in national elections in 1984.

“Liechtenstein has a history of being the last when it comes to women’s rights,” she said. “I had hoped that we wouldn’t be the last in abortion rights as well, but it doesn’t look good at the moment.”

The campaign had managed to chalk up a few successes, she said, pointing to how it had chipped away at the decades-long taboo in talking about the topic in the nation.

Even so, Alvarez-Hummel worried that the estimated 40 women a year who are forced to carry out the procedure abroad would now face greater stigma and more deeply entrenched taboos.

“You live in a country where it is forbidden, where the prince who lives in a castle made sure it stayed forbidden,” she said. “The one time he used his veto was against this – I can only imagine how difficult it must be for them to know this.”
output.standfirst: Hereditary Prince Alois says he is open to lifting Liechtenstein’s ban on abortion information, after vetoing a bill – passed by parliament and backed by a quarter of voters – to decriminalise abortion.

output.headline: Woman told mother Brand raped her despite her screaming in pain, court hears
output.bodyHtml:
A woman told her mother that Russell Brand had raped her and “didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain”, a court has heard.

The woman also told a colleague she was “bleeding everywhere” and that Brand had shouted at her, saying, “Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets”, Southwark crown court heard on Thursday.

The woman told her parents, friends, boyfriend and a sexual health nurse about the alleged attack and several encouraged her to go to the police but she feared she would not be believed, the court was told.

Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. The 51-year-old denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

The court heard on Thursday from 24 witnesses connected to the woman, who alleges Brand anally raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. She alleges they had consensual vaginal sex before the comedian “flipped” her over and raped her.

Giving evidence over video link, a friend who had accompanied the woman to the gig said the comedian had signed off the show by saying: “If you see me out in the foyer and you think ‘I really fancy him and would like to have sex with him, but I can’t because it is Russell Brand’, you probably can … my age range is from 16 to death.”

The woman’s parents said their daughter had confided in them shortly after the alleged attack and feared she had contracted HIV. In a witness statement read by the junior prosecution counsel, Suki Dhadda, the woman’s mother said: “She said he forced anal sex on her and didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain and asked him to stop.”

Her father said his daughter told him: “They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted. I turned to her in the car and asked her if she asked him to stop, and she said ‘yes’ several times. It was then I said to her: ‘You have been raped, that’s rape.’”

The woman’s colleague told the court the alleged victim was “ashen, greyish, and looked ill” when describing shortly after the alleged attack how Brand had “really fucking hurt” her.

The colleague told the court: “She described that he got aggressive and pushed her down on the bed and she couldn’t breathe and she was trying to say stop because it was hurting her. I said: ‘Did you stay stop?’ and she said: ‘Yes, multiple times.’”

Recalling the woman’s account, the colleague added: “She was bleeding everywhere, from her anus, and he shouted at her, Mr Brand, he said: ‘Look what you’ve done to my fucking sheets’ or something like that, and she was very embarrassed.”

The witness said she told the woman she had been raped and encouraged her to go to the police but the woman replied: “They won’t believe me. I went to his house.”

A friend of the woman also told the court that she had encouraged her to go to the police, but the alleged victim “felt it wasn’t worth it”.

“She didn’t think she would be believed,” the witness said. A couple of days after the alleged attack the woman told her Brand had treated her “like an animal”. “She was in a lot of pain and asked him to stop anally raping her and he wouldn’t,” her friend said.

Another friend recalled how the woman had told her that Brand called her “dirty” after the alleged rape and how “he had gone from being charming to violent and cold-hearted”.

The friend added the woman’s “face was as white as a sheet” when she bumped into Brand at the Edinburgh festival in the summer after the alleged attack.

In her witness statement read to the court, the friend said she was at the festival when Brand was “pinging off” the woman’s phone with messages and calls.

“She was concerned that he had tracked her down because he was still pursuing her in the lead-up to that. He was becoming increasingly frustrated that she wasn’t responding to him. I could see he really want to see her and have sex with her from the using crude sexual language in the messages,” the friend said.

In 2024, the woman confided in another friend about the festival encounter and said she had replied to one of Brand’s messages saying: “I wouldn’t treat a dog the way you treated me.”

Another friend spoke of the toll the alleged rape had had on the woman, saying she had been a “bright, confident and bubbly girl” but the encounter with Brand had “changed her”. “It’s like she lost respect for herself after that day. She blamed herself for what happened,” the friend said in a witness statement.

The woman’s former boyfriend told the court that she had not wanted to have anal sex but had “surrendered”. In cross-examination by Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC the man was asked about a witness statement he had given in June 2025 in which he said the woman had “come round” to having anal sex.

The trial continues.
output.standfirst: Parents, colleagues and others encouraged her to go to the police, but she was worried she would not be believed, the court heard.

output.headline: Bond casting nears finish line as finalists screen-test this weekend
output.bodyHtml:
The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.

According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety, citing several sources, a group of actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.

The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

Related: The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world

Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. The Peaky Blinders writer Steven Knight will pen the script.

The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”

In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”

Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.

“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”

It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.

Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.
output.standfirst: Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are reportedly among the actors in the running to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment.
